expectation over transformation
elements.text: A method for strengthening adversarial examples to remain adversarial under image transformations that occur in the real world, such as angle and viewpoint changes. EOT models these perturbations within the optimization procedure. Rather than optimizing the log-likelihood of a single example, EOT uses a chosen distribution of transformation functions that take an input controlled by the adversary to the “true” input perceived by the classifier.

elements.title: formal methods
elements.text: A mathematically rigorous technique for the specification, development, and verification of software systems.

elements.title: label limit
elements.text: A capability with which an attacker does not control the labels of training samples in supervised learning.

elements.title: model control
elements.text: A capability with which an attacker can control the machine learning model parameters.

elements.title: query access
elements.text: A capability with which an attacker can issue queries to a trained machine learning model and obtain predictions or generations.

elements.title: source code control
elements.text: A capability with which an attacker controls the source code of a machine learning algorithm.

elements.title: testing data control
elements.text: A capability with which an attacker controls the testing data input to the machine learning model.

elements.title: training data control
elements.text: A capability in which an attacker controls some or all of the training data of a machine learning model.

elements.title: functional attack
elements.text: An adversarial attack that is optimized for a set of data in a domain rather than per data point.

elements.title: adversarial example
elements.text: A modified testing sample that induces misclassification or misbehavior of a machine learning model at deployment time.

elements.title: classification
elements.text: The task of predicting which of a set of discrete categories an input belongs to.

elements.title: convolutional neural networks
elements.text: A class of feed-forward neural networks that include at least one convolutional layer, referred to as CNNs. In convolutional layers, feature detectors (known as kernels or filters) detect specific features across the input data. CNNs are primarily used for processing grid-like data, such as images, and are particularly effective for tasks like image classification, object detection, and image segmentation.

elements.title: data poisoning
elements.text: A POISONING ATTACKS in which an adversary controls part of the training data.

elements.title: poisoning attacks
elements.text: Adversarial attacks in which an adversary interferes with a model during its TRAINING STAGE, such as by inserting malicious training data (DATA POISONING) or modifying the training process itself (MODEL POISONING).

elements.title: training stage
elements.text: The stage of a machine learning pipeline in which a model learns parameters that minimize its error against an objective function based on training data.

elements.title: deployment stage
elements.text: The stage of the machine learning pipeline in which a model is deployed into a live or real-world environment for use, such as being integrated into an enterprise application or made available to end users through an API.

elements.title: discriminative
elements.text: A type of machine learning method that learns to discriminate between classes.

elements.title: ensemble learning
elements.text: A type of a meta machine learning approach that combines the predictions of several models to improve performance.

elements.title: federated learning
elements.text: A type of machine learning in which a model is trained in a decentralized fashion using multiple data sources without pooling or combining the data in any centralized location. Federated learning allows entities or devices to collaboratively train a global model by exchanging model updates without directly sharing the data that each entity controls.

elements.title: logistic regression
elements.text: A type of linear classifier that predicts the probability of an observation being part of a class.

elements.title: model poisoning
elements.text: A POISONING ATTACKS which operates through MODEL CONTROL.

elements.title: regression
elements.text: A type of supervised machine learning model that is trained on data, including numerical labels (i.e., response variables). Types of regression algorithms include linear regression, polynomial regression, and various non-linear regression methods.

elements.title: reinforcement learning
elements.text: A type of machine learning in which a model learns to optimize its behavior according to a reward function by interacting with and receiving feedback from an environment.

elements.title: semi-supervised learning
elements.text: A type of machine learning in which a small number of training samples are labeled, while the majority are unlabeled.

elements.title: supervised learning
elements.text: A type of machine learning in which a model learns to predict explicit (often human-generated) labels or output values for data.

elements.title: support vector machines
elements.text: Models that implement a decision function in the form of a hyperplane that serves to separate (i.e., classify) observations that belong to one class from another based on patterns of information about those observations (i.e., features).

elements.title: unsupervised learning
elements.text: A type of machine learning in which a model learns based on patterns in unlabeled data, such as learning a function to cluster or group data points.

elements.title: attribute inference attacks
elements.text: An attack against machine learning models that infers sensitive attributes of a training data record, given partial knowledge about the record.

elements.title: availability breakdown
elements.text: In the AML context, a disruption of the ability of other users or processes to obtain timely and reliable access to an AI system’s outputs or functionality.

elements.title: backdoor pattern
elements.text: A transformation or insertion applied to a data sample that triggers an adversary-specified behavior in a model that has been subject to a backdoor poisoning attack. For example, in computer vision, an adversary could poison a model such that the insertion of a square of white pixels induces a desired target label.

elements.title: backdoor poisoning attack
elements.text: A poisoning attack that causes a model to perform an adversary selected behavior in response to inputs that follow a particular BACKDOOR PATTERN.

elements.title: data confidentiality
elements.text: A well-established concept in cybersecurity referring to the protection of sensitive information from unauthorized access and disclosure.

elements.title: data privacy attacks
elements.text: Attacks against machine learning models that extract sensitive information about training data.

elements.title: data reconstruction
elements.text: Privacy attacks that reconstruct sensitive data in a model’s training data from aggregate information.

elements.title: energy-latency attack
elements.text: An attack that exploits the performance dependency on hardware and model optimizations to negate the effects of hardware optimizations, increase computational latency, increase hardware temperature, and massively increase the amount of energy consumed.

elements.title: integrity violation
elements.text: In the AML context, an AI system being forced to misperform against its intended objectives, producing outputs or predictions that align with the attacker’s objective.

elements.title: membership-inference attack
elements.text: A data privacy attack to determine whether a data sample was part of the training set of a machine learning model.

elements.title: model extraction
elements.text: A type of privacy attack that extracts details of the model architecture and/or parameters.

elements.title: model privacy attacks
elements.text: An attack against machine learning models to extract sensitive information about the model.

elements.title: privacy compromise
elements.text: In the AML context, the unauthorized access of restricted or proprietary information that is part of an AI system, including information about a model’s training data, weights or architecture; or sensitive information that the model accesses such as the knowledge base of a GenAI RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION (RAG) application.

elements.title: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
elements.text: A type of GenAI system in which a model is paired with a separate information retrieval system (or  “knowledge base”). Based on a user query, the RAG system identifies relevant information within the knowledge base and provides it to the GenAI model in context for the model to use in formulating its response. RAG systems allow the internal knowledge of a GenAI model to be modified without the need for retraining.

elements.title: property inference
elements.text: A data privacy attack that infers a global property about the training data of a machine learning model.

elements.title: targeted poisoning attack
elements.text: A poisoning attack that changes the prediction on a small number of targeted samples.

elements.title: training data extraction
elements.text: The ability of an attacker to extract the training data of a generative model by prompting the model with specific inputs.

elements.title: shadow mode
elements.text: A model that imitates the behavior of the target model. The training datasets and the truth about membership in these datasets are known for these models. Typically, the attack model is trained on the labeled inputs and outputs of the shadow model.

elements.title: machine unlearning
elements.text: A technique that involves selectively removing the influences of specific training data points from a trained machine learning model, such as to remove unwanted capabilities or knowledge in a foundation model, or to enable a user to request the removal of their records from a model. Efficient approximate unlearning techniques may not require retraining the ML model from scratch.

elements.title: label flipping
elements.text: A type of data poisoning attack in which an adversary is restricted to changing the training labels.

elements.title: diffusion models
elements.text: A class of latent variable generative models consisting of three major components: a forward process, a reverse process, and a sampling procedure. The goal of the diffusion model is to learn a diffusion process that generates the probability distribution of a given dataset. It is widely used in computer vision on a variety of tasks, including image denoising, inpainting, super-resolution, and image generation.

elements.title: generative pre-trained transformer (GPT)
elements.text: A family of machine learning models based on the transformer architecture that are pre-trained through SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING on large data sets of unlabeled text. This is the current predominant architecture for large language models.

elements.title: out-of-distribution
elements.text: Data that was collected at a different time and possibly under different conditions or in a different environment than the data collected to train the model.

elements.title: multimodal models
elements.text: A model that processes and relates information from multiple sensory modalities that each represent primary human channels of communication and sensation, such as vision and touch.

elements.title: red teaming
elements.text: In the AI context, means a structured testing effort, often adopting adversarial methods, to find flaws and vulnerabilities in an AI system, including unforeseen or undesirable system behaviors or potential risks associated with the misuse of the system.

elements.title: trojan
elements.text: In the machine learning context, a malicious modification to a model that is difficult to detect, may appear harmless, but that can alter the intended function of the system upon a signal from an attacker to cause a malicious behavior desired by the attacker. For Trojan attacks to be effective, the trigger must be rare in the normal operating environment so that it does not affect the normal effectiveness of the AI and raise the suspicions of users. In the machine learning context, trojan may be used interchangeably with backdoor pattern.

elements.title: adversarial machine learning
elements.text: Attacks that exploit the statistical, data-based nature of machine learning systems.

elements.title: feedforward neural networks
elements.text: Artificial neural networks in which the connections between nodes is from one layer to the next and do not form a cycle.

elements.title: foundation model
elements.text: In generative AI, models trained on broad data using SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING that can be adapted such as through fine-tuning for a variety of downstream tasks.

elements.title: agent
elements.text: Software programs that can interact with their environment, receive information, and undertake self-directed action sin service of a larger, externally-specified goal.

elements.title: direct prompt injection
elements.text: A DIRECT PROMPTING ATTACK in which the attacker exploits PROMPT INJECTION.

elements.title: prompt injection
elements.text: An attack which exploits the concatenation of untrusted input with a prompt constructed by a higher-trust party such as the application designer.

elements.title: direct prompting attack
elements.text: In the generative AI context, an attack conducted by the primary user of the system through QUERY ACCESS (e.g., as opposed to through RESOURCE CONTROL).

elements.title: resource control
elements.text: A capability in which an attacker controls one or more external resources consumed by a machine learning model at inference time, particularly for GenAI systems such as retrieval-augmented generation applications.

elements.title: fine-tuning
elements.text: The process of adapting a pre-trained model to perform specific tasks or specialize in a particular domain. This phase follows the initial pre-training phase and involves further training the model on task-specific data. This is often a supervised learning task.

elements.title: pre-training
elements.text: A component of the TRAINING STAGE in which a model learns general patterns, features, and relationships from vast amounts of unlabeled data, such as through SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING. Pre-training can equip models with knowledge of general features or patterns which may be useful in downstream tasks (see FOUNDATION MODEL), and can be followed with additional training or fine-tuning that specializes the model for a specific downstream task.

elements.title: self-supervised learning
elements.text: A type of machine learning that relies on generating implicit labels from unstructured data rather than relying on explicit, human-created labels. Self-supervised learning tasks are constructed to allow the true labels to be automatically inferred from the training data (enabling the use of large-scale training data) and to require models to capture essential features or relationships within the data to solve them. For example, a common self-supervised learning task is providing a model with partial data with the task to accurately generate the remainder.

elements.title: indirect prompt injection
elements.text: A type of PROMPT INJECTION executed through RESOURCE CONTROL rather than through user-provided input as in a DIRECT PROMPT INJECTION.

elements.title: jailbreak
elements.text: A DIRECT PROMPTING ATTACK intended to circumvent restrictions placed on model outputs, such as circumventing refusal behavior to enable misuse.

elements.title: prompt extraction
elements.text: An attack that tries to divulge the system prompt or other information in the context of a large language model that would normally be hidden from a user.

elements.title: system prompt
elements.text: Application-specific instructions provided in-context to a GenAI system by the model developer or application designer. System prompts are typically prepended to other input, and may be higher-trust than other forms of input.

elements.title: area under the curve
elements.text: A measure of the ability of a classifier to distinguish between classes in machine learning. A higher AUC means that a model performs better when distinguishing between the two classes. AUC measures the entire two-dimensional area under the RECEIVER OPERATING CHARACTERISTIC (ROC) curve.

elements.title: receiver operating characteristic (ROC)
elements.text: A curve that plots the true positive rate versus the false positive rate for a classifier.

elements.title: generative adversarial networks
elements.text: A machine learning framework in which two neural networks contest with each other in the form of a zero-sum game, where one agent’s gain is another agent’s loss. A GAN learns to generate new data with the same statistics as the training set. See for further details.

elements.title: graph neural network
elements.text: A neural network designed to process graph-structured data. GNNs perform optimizable transformations on graph attributes(e.g., nodes, edges, global context) while preserving graph symmetries such as permutation invariance. GNNs utilize a “graph-in, graph-out” architecture that takes an input graph with information and progressively transforms it into an output graph with the same connectivity as that of the input graph.

elements.title: hidden Markov model
elements.text: A Markov model in which the system being modeled is assumed to be a Markov process with unobservable states. The model provides an observable process whose outcomes are influenced by the outcomes of a Markov model in a known way. An HMM can be used to describe the evolution of observable events that depend on internal factors that are not directly observable. In machine learning, it is assumed that the internal state of a model is hidden but not its hyperparameters.

elements.title: rowhammer attack
elements.text: A software-based fault-injection attack that exploits dynamic random-access memory disturbance errors via user-space applications and allows the attacker to infer information about certain victim secrets stored in memory cells. Mounting this attack requires the attacker to control a user-space unprivileged process that runs on the same machine as the victim’s machine learning model.

elements.title: side channel
elements.text: Allows an attacker to infer information about a secret by observing the nonfunctional characteristics of a program (e.g., execution time or memory) or measuring or exploiting the indirect coincidental effects of the system or its hardware (e.g., power consumption variation, electromagnetic emanations) while the program is executing. Most commonly, such attacks aim to exfiltrate sensitive information, including cryptographic keys.

elements.title: misuse enablement
elements.text: In the AML context, a circumvention of technical restrictions imposed by the AI system’s owner on its use, such as restrictions designed to prevent a GenAI system from producing outputs that could cause harm to others.

elements.title: fine-tuning circumvention
elements.text: Fine-tuning to remove model refusal behavior or other model level safety interventions.
